title: Acute pancreatitis
subject: gastroenterology
summary: Diagnose with 2 of 3 criteria, grade severity by revised Atlanta (persistent organ failure over 48 hours = severe), give moderate goal-directed Ringer lactate, feed orally early, avoid prophylactic antibiotics, ERCP within 24 hours only for cholangitis, and cholecystectomy before discharge in mild gallstone pancreatitis.

sections.title: Diagnosis and cause
items: Diagnose with 2 of 3: typical pain (constant epigastric, often radiating to the back), serum lipase or amylase above 3 times the upper limit of normal, or characteristic imaging. Lipase is preferred over amylase.
Do not do CT at admission to grade severity. Reserve CT for diagnostic uncertainty or failure to improve after 48 to 72 hours.
Transabdominal ultrasound in every patient to look for gallstones; repeat if the first scan is inconclusive.
Commonest causes: gallstones (40 to 70%) and alcohol (25 to 35%). Without either, measure triglycerides: above 1,000 mg/dL (11.3 mmol/L) makes hypertriglyceridaemia the likely cause.
Age above 40 with no clear cause: consider a pancreatic tumour. Idiopathic cases: repeat ultrasound, MRI/MRCP or EUS.

sections.title: Severity and triage
items: Revised Atlanta: mild = no organ failure and no local or systemic complications; moderately severe = transient organ failure (resolves within 48 hours), local complications or exacerbation of co-morbid disease; severe = persistent organ failure beyond 48 hours.

Organ failure (ACG 2024): shock (systolic BP below 90 mmHg), PaO2 below 60 mmHg, creatinine above 2 mg/dL after rehydration, or a modified Marshall score of 2 or more in the respiratory, cardiovascular or renal system.
Risk factors for a severe course: SIRS, high or rising urea (BUN) or haematocrit, obesity, older age, comorbidity, altered mental state, pleural effusions or infiltrates.
Scores and imaging alone predict severity poorly; stay vigilant for organ failure during the first 48 hours even in apparently mild disease.
Admit patients with SIRS or organ failure to a monitored bed or ICU. Baseline: CBC, urea, creatinine, electrolytes, calcium, LFT, triglycerides, glucose, blood gas where indicated.

sections.title: Fluids and analgesia (first 24 to 48 hours)
items: Use Ringer lactate rather than 0.9% saline.
Moderate goal-directed resuscitation: 1.5 mL/kg/h; give a 10 mL/kg bolus first only if hypovolaemic (ACG 2024, WATERFALL).
Aggressive fluids (20 mL/kg bolus then 3 mL/kg/h) caused more fluid overload without better outcomes in WATERFALL; avoid them.
Reassess volume status within 6 hours and repeatedly over 24 to 48 hours (heart rate, BP, urine output, urea and haematocrit), aiming for a falling urea. Fluids help most in the first 24 hours.
Extra caution with cardiac or renal disease and in older patients; watch for pulmonary oedema and abdominal compartment syndrome.
Give adequate analgesia, using opioids when simple analgesia is insufficient.

sections.title: Nutrition and antibiotics
items: Mild pancreatitis: start oral feeding within 24 to 48 hours as tolerated, beginning with a low-fat solid diet rather than stepwise clear liquids.
Moderately severe or severe: enteral feeding if oral intake is inadequate; nasogastric route is acceptable (comparable to nasojejunal). Avoid parenteral nutrition unless enteral feeding fails.
No prophylactic antibiotics, even in severe pancreatitis or sterile necrosis. Treat proven infections (cholangitis, bacteraemia, pneumonia, urinary infection).

Suspected infected necrosis (clinical deterioration or gas in the collection, typically after 10 to 14 days): antibiotics that penetrate necrosis (carbapenem, quinolone, cephalosporin with metronidazole). No routine antifungals and no fine-needle aspiration.

sections.title: Gallstone pancreatitis
items: Cholangitis: ERCP within 24 hours.
No cholangitis: medical therapy rather than early ERCP. If a bile duct stone is suspected without cholangitis or jaundice, confirm by MRCP or EUS before ERCP.
Mild gallstone pancreatitis: cholecystectomy during the same admission, before discharge.
High-risk ERCP patients: rectal indomethacin 100 mg before or immediately after ERCP to prevent post-ERCP pancreatitis; consider a pancreatic duct stent.

sections.title: Necrosis and complications
items: Stable pancreatic necrosis: delay any drainage or necrosectomy, preferably 4 weeks, to allow the collection wall to mature; antibiotics may avoid or delay intervention in infected necrosis.

When intervention is needed, prefer minimally invasive (endoscopic or percutaneous step-up) over open surgery. Unstable infected necrosis may need urgent intervention: involve a pancreatic multidisciplinary team.
Escalate to ICU for persistent organ failure, rising oxygen need, shock or AKI.

sections.title: Prevent recurrence
items: Alcohol-related: brief intervention and referral for alcohol use disorder at every admission.
Hypertriglyceridaemia: repeat fasting triglycerides about 1 month after discharge and treat the lipid disorder.
Second episode with no identifiable cause in a patient fit for surgery: consider cholecystectomy.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Early CT for severity, which adds little and may miss necrosis that evolves later.
Large-volume aggressive fluids beyond the first 24 to 48 hours.
Routine prophylactic carbapenems for severe or necrotising pancreatitis.
Keeping mild pancreatitis nil by mouth, or discharging mild gallstone pancreatitis without cholecystectomy.

drugs.name: Ringer lactate
drugs.dose: 1.5 mL/kg/h IV; 10 mL/kg IV bolus first only if hypovolaemic
drugs.notes: Reassess at 6 hours and over 24 to 48 hours. Reduce in cardiac or renal disease.

drugs.name: Indomethacin (rectal)
drugs.dose: 100 mg rectally, single dose before or immediately after ERCP
drugs.notes: Prevention of post-ERCP pancreatitis in high-risk patients.

drugs.name: Meropenem (infected necrosis only)
drugs.notes: Example of a necrosis-penetrating agent; adjust for renal function and local resistance. Not for prophylaxis.

sources.title: American College of Gastroenterology Guidelines: Management of Acute Pancreatitis (Tenner et al., Am J Gastroenterol)
Aggressive or Moderate Fluid Resuscitation in Acute Pancreatitis (de-Madaria et al.)
